title: Abeilles Inc. (Oct 2014 TCC) Tax Court of Canada Case
subject: TCC appeal on whether shop-floor process development qualified as SR&ED and whether contemporaneous records are mandatory.
summary: Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313) is a Tax Court of Canada ruling that shop-floor process development by Canadian manufacturers can qualify as SR&ED experimental development under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. It held that contemporaneous documentation is not a statutory condition for SR&ED recognition and allowed the appeal with costs.
metaDescription: Discover the October 2014 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Abeilles Inc. and its relevance to Canadian R&D tax claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Overview of the Ruling and Strategic Significance

On October 23, 2014, the Honourable Justice Gaston Jorré of the Tax Court of Canada (Cour canadienne de l'impôt) delivered a landmark judgment in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen (2014 TCC 313 / 2014 CCI 313, 2014 DTC 1219, Docket No. 2011-2054(IT)G), allowing the taxpayer's appeal in full with costs. Following a trial held over five days in June and July 2013 (June 18, 19, 20, 26 and July 11, 2013) in Montréal, where the appellant was represented by Julie Patenaude and the Crown by Christina Ham, the Court allowed the appeal from the reassessment issued by the Minister of National Revenue (ministre du Revenu national) on January 27, 2011. That reassessment had reduced the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (recherche scientifique et développement expérimental — SR&ED / RS&DE) tax credit claimed by the appellant in respect of four industrial process development projects for the 2009 taxation year. Justice Jorré referred the matter back to the Minister for reconsideration and reassessment on the basis that Projects 2007-01, 2007-02, 2009-01, and 2009-02 constituted eligible experimental development within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (Loi de l'impôt sur le revenu — ITA / LIR).

Within Canadian tax jurisprudence, Les Abeilles stands as an important judicial authority on shop-floor experimental development (développement expérimental en usine), addressing projects aimed at conceiving, adapting, or optimizing automated manufacturing, assembly, and industrial packaging processes rather than fabricating a standalone commercial product. The decision establishes four foundational legal principles for Canadian SR&ED practitioners and corporate claimants. First, the ruling affirms the supremacy of the statutory text over administrative policy, holding that internal administrative guidelines published by the Canada Revenue Agency (Agence du revenu du Canada — CRA / ARC) cannot impose legal prerequisites that do not exist in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act or the Income Tax Regulations (Règlement de l'impôt sur le revenu). Second, the Court clarified the exact evidentiary role of contemporaneous documentation, ruling at paragraph 94 that while the existence and content of contemporaneous records are relevant to resolving factual disputes and assessing weight, neither the Income Tax Act nor the Regulations make contemporaneous documentation—or contemporaneous documents with specific content—a condition precedent to the recognition of SR&ED. Third, Justice Jorré distinguished experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), which requires an effort to achieve technological advancement (progrès technologique), from basic or applied research under paragraphs 248(1)(a) and (b), which require the advancement of scientific knowledge. Consequently, the Court found technological uncertainty where the taxpayer did not know at the outset how it would achieve its specific production objectives (such as cycle time, flexibility and quality) and could not find a ready-made solution through its client's knowledge network, its suppliers or Web searches, so that the work could not be characterized as the application of standard procedures or routine engineering. Fourth, the Court mandated holistic project evaluation over reductionist deconstruction, holding that each project must be considered globally in the year at issue rather than test by test, and that, while experimental development must be carried out in the year in question, the history of a project that began in a previous year may be examined in determining whether such work was carried out in that year.
Factual and Operational Context of the Taxpayer

The appellant, Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. ("Les Abeilles"), is an industrial subcontracting, sub-assembly, and packaging corporation located in Montréal, Québec. Founded in 1987 by the mother of Serge Caouette—who served as the company's president and sole shareholder at the time of the hearing—the corporation initially provided packaging and printing finishing services to tobacco manufacturers. When restrictions on the advertising of tobacco products forced the company to diversify, Les Abeilles continued its printing finishing activities, began providing packaging services to businesses in the food and cosmetic industries, and broadened its activities in the industrial sector by starting the assembly of mechanical components, which led to its sub-assembly work for a household dryer manufacturer.

In its appliance sub-assembly division, Les Abeilles operated in close industrial integration with Mabe / General Electric ("Mabe/GE"), which assembled household clothes dryers in the Montréal region. General Electric held 49% of the shares of Mabe and initiated the collaboration between Mabe and the appellant, although the contracts were concluded between Mabe and the appellant; Mabe/GE was not the appellant's sole client, as Project 2009-02 had no connection to Mabe/GE. Operating an industrial sub-assembly facility in Montréal exposed both Les Abeilles and Mabe/GE to intense international cost competition from lower-wage manufacturing jurisdictions in Mexico and Asia. As Justice Jorré explicitly noted at paragraph 11 and footnote 5 of the reasons for judgment, the projects were aimed at increasing the efficiency of the appellant's work without excessive expense that it could not support while remaining competitive, and it was precisely this search for efficiency that allowed the appellant and its client to avoid the offshoring of dryer manufacturing; the Court added that the Canadian economy stands to gain from having as many companies as possible undertake such efforts, which could help prevent offshoring and perhaps even encourage reshoring.

Les Abeilles initiated systematic process development projects in 2002 and filed its first SR&ED claim in 2003, submitting several project claims annually thereafter. For the 2009 taxation year, the corporation submitted SR&ED applications covering six projects. Following its audit, the CRA approved two of the projects and disallowed the remaining four, reducing the credit in respect of claimed expenditures of approximately $481,000 in salaries and approximately $5,300 in materials (based on the per-project amounts set out in the reasons for judgment). Two of the disallowed projects (2007-01 and 2007-02) were multi-year experimental development initiatives commenced in 2007 that the CRA had previously audited and allowed as eligible SR&ED in prior taxation years, whereas the other two disallowed projects (2009-01 and 2009-02) were newly initiated in 2009.

headers: Technical Objectives and Target Operational Metrics

cells: Project 2007-01
Development of a new assembling process for motors for dryers (Appliance Sub-Assembly Division)
Initiated in 2007; continued into 2009 (accepted as SR&ED by CRA in prior tax years)

Make it possible to assemble all the different types (families) of motors on the same production line without stopping the line to change models (eliminating the less efficient assembly carousels), and reduce the motor sub-assembly cycle time from approximately 14 seconds at the beginning of 2009 to 9 seconds while meeting Mabe/GE's quality standard of a maximum of 300 rejects per million sub-assemblies; the 2009 work included recalibrating electronic relays to prevent contact fusing, testing actuator positioners, and validating universal hubs on the pulley press (by year-end, all motor families could be assembled on the line and the cycle time was approximately 10 seconds).
32 tests; over 9,000 person-hours (9,367.5 hours per Appendix B); approximately $137,000 in salaries and $1,300 in materials; Mabe/GE supplied the components free of charge.
Project 2007-02
Development of a new assembling process for heating elements for dryers (Appliance Sub-Assembly Division)
Initiated in 2007; continued into 2009 (accepted as SR&ED by CRA in prior tax years)

Achieve a 7-second sub-assembly cycle time (from approximately 9.6 seconds at the beginning of 2009), meet a quality standard of fewer than 300 rejects per million, and integrate new models of heating elements on the same line; the problems addressed included excessive proximity between the heating element and the housing (solved by a cylinder system, the third of three successive solutions after a manual one requiring a special tool and a hybrid one with a thumb detector) and false rejects at the test station caused by the impact between the element and the stop (solved by a linear motion stop); at year-end the cycle time was 8.9 seconds and the quality standard had yet to be met.
19 tests; over 7,500 person-hours; approximately $110,000 in salaries and $1,100 in materials; Mabe/GE supplied heating element components free of charge.
Project 2009-01
Development of a new assembling process for control panels using pull flow with electronic sequencing (Appliance Sub-Assembly Division)
New project initiated in 2009

Engineer a single assembly line utilizing pull-flow and electronic sequencing (the "surgeon approach") capable of producing 174 control panel variations based on 600 possible components, delivering the particular variation ordered within four hours following the order, producing the panels much faster than Mabe, and changing from one model to another within 30 seconds while meeting a quality standard of fewer than 300 rejects per million.
22 shop-floor experimental tests; over 9,000 person-hours of labour; approximately $160,000 in salaries and $2,600 in materials; components supplied by Mabe/GE.
Project 2009-02
High-speed synchronization for the application of secondary components on a print component (Print Finishing Division)
New project initiated in 2009

Increase secondary component application speed by over 80% (from 6,000 to 11,000 applications per hour) while re-engineering the secondary feeder to accommodate larger component formats and add new secondary components.
13 experimental tests; >6,000 person-hours of labour; ~$74,000 in salaries and $300 in materials.

body.text: Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework in Canada

The Canadian SR&ED tax incentive program operates through a dual statutory mechanism under the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)). Section 37 permits taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to deduct current SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year or carry those pools forward indefinitely to subsequent taxation years, while subsections 127(5) and 127(9) provide an Investment Tax Credit (crédit d'impôt à l'investissement — ITC / CII). For a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (société privée sous contrôle canadien — CCPC / SPCC), the federal program provided, for the 2009 taxation year at issue, a 35% refundable ITC on the first $3 million of qualified expenditures and a 20% ITC on excess amounts (the general rate was later reduced to 15% for taxation years ending after 2013), while other Canadian corporations received the general-rate non-refundable ITC; for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, assented to March 26, 2026) has raised the expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% credit to $6 million and extended it to eligible Canadian public corporations. In Québec, the federal incentives were complemented by a refundable provincial R&D salary tax credit, which was replaced, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, by the refundable tax credit for research, innovation and commercialization (designated by Revenu Québec as the tax credit for R&D, innovation and pre-commercialization — CRIC), at a basic rate of 20%, increased to 30% on up to $1 million of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold. Following legislative amendments applicable to expenditures incurred after 2013, capital equipment expenditures and capital lease costs ceased to be eligible for SR&ED treatment, focusing claims on salaries, wages, subcontractors, and materials consumed or transformed, although the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 has since restored the eligibility of capital expenditures for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024.

The statutory gateway to both section 37 expenditure pools and section 127 investment tax credits is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. As parsed by Justice Jorré at paragraphs 6 through 8 of the decision, the preamble of subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" that falls into one of three substantive categories: paragraph (a) covers basic research (recherche pure), namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; paragraph (b) covers applied research (recherche appliquée), namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and paragraph (c) covers experimental development (développement expérimental), namely work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement (dans l'intérêt du progrès technologique) for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto (l'amélioration, même légère, de ceux qui existent).

Under paragraph (d) of subsection 248(1), the definition encompasses support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of core research or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) exclude specific routine and commercial activities from SR&ED eligibility, most notably paragraph (f), which excludes quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes, and paragraph (i), which excludes the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process.

To apply subsection 248(1) consistently, Canadian courts utilize the five-part jurisprudential test formulated by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC)) and approved by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087), as summarized by that Court in CW Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393). That analytical framework asks: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed.

In Les Abeilles, Justice Jorré noted that while the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria provide a vital analytical structure, they are not absolute statutory replacements for the text of the Income Tax Act itself. Drawing on the Federal Court of Appeal's statement in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087) that systematic research may be inferred where it is established that such research led to a technological advancement, and on Judge Archambault's evidentiary ruling in 116736 Canada inc. v. Canada ([1998] ACI No. 478 (QL)), and having identified the central issue as whether the four projects constitute "experimental development" (paragraph 138), Justice Jorré framed the analysis at paragraph 140 around two questions: whether the projects were undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement, and whether they were undertaken for the purpose of creating new processes, including incremental improvements. Answering both questions in the affirmative for all four projects, the Court allowed the appeal with costs.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A comprehensive legal and technical diagnosis of Les Abeilles requires examining two distinct sets of deficiencies: first, the taxpayer's audit-stage documentation and operational presentation vulnerabilities that triggered the CRA's initial reassessment and led to a dispute that ran from the Minister's reassessment of January 27, 2011 to the Tax Court's judgment of October 23, 2014; and second, the Crown's fatal legal, methodological, and expert-witness failures at trial that contributed to the Tax Court of Canada's decision to allow the appeal and refer the reassessment back to the Minister on the basis that all four projects constituted experimental development.
Taxpayer Audit-Stage Vulnerabilities That Triggered the Dispute
1. Absence of Formal SR&ED-Dedicated Logbooks and Fragmented ERP Records

Although Les Abeilles ultimately prevailed in Court, its claim was supported largely by detailed project and test descriptions that, as the Court acknowledged, were in many cases not contemporaneous, rather than by formal contemporaneous engineering notebooks or SR&ED technical reports recording hypotheses, experimental variables, and analytical conclusions in a format immediately familiar to CRA auditors. Instead, the corporation's contemporaneous records were dispersed across operational database tables inside its enterprise management system. Specifically, the contemporaneous portion of the record in Exhibit A-12 included three tabs derived from the appellant's database, in which the data was collected as activities were being carried out: a chronological activity table ("Chronology 2009"), a barcode-scanned employee time-tracking ledger ("Data" tab recording employee names and identification numbers, exact arrival and departure timestamps, dates, and specific project and test numbers), and a tab entitled "Perf Dos", supplemented by Exhibits A-3 and A-4, contemporaneous documents containing certain limited information about the projects. At the audit stage, the CRA's scientific advisor, Dr. Steven Kooi, concluded in his technical review report dated November 18, 2010 that, except for Project 2009-01, there was no technological obstacle because the issues were engineering challenges resolved through current standard engineering practice, while for part of Project 2009-01 he found the work "uncorroborated" and provided no opinion; that audit report made no mention of a lack of contemporaneous documents or of the absence of a log, and it was only in his expert report and testimony that Dr. Kooi asserted that no contemporaneous log or logbook had been kept—an assertion the Court could not understand given the "Chronology 2009" tab of Exhibit A-12, which is a form of log kept contemporaneously in the appellant's database. The taxpayer's detailed descriptions of the projects and tests, many of which were not contemporaneous (and which Dr. Kooi had himself consulted and relied on in preparing his November 18, 2010 audit report), were filed in evidence by consent and their content was not disputed, so the Court treated them as correctly reflecting the purpose and accomplishments of the projects and what was done during testing.
2. Shop-Floor Operational Overlap and Deviation Classification Ambiguity

All four disputed projects were conducted directly on industrial assembly and printing finishing lines rather than within an isolated laboratory environment. To manage non-standard events on its lines, Les Abeilles classified operational "deviations" (écarts) into three internal categories: (a) component substitution, (b) change in engineering, and (c) experimental development. While only the third category of deviations was claimed as SR&ED, conducting experimental trials on an interconnected assembly line required full operational staffing—as Mr. Caouette testified at paragraph 36, it took at least as many employees to conduct a shop-floor test as it did to run regular commercial production. Consequently, Project 2009-01 accumulated over 9,000 person-hours across 22 tests, Project 2009-02 accumulated close to 6,000 person-hours across 13 tests, and in Project 2007-02, test 2282 alone accounted for 627.25 person-hours of work by 28 persons involved at different times over the course of the test. Because the appellant's per-test documents reported "hours of tests" rather than "person-hours of work spent on the test," Dr. Kooi, in his expert report, interpreted those figures literally as hours of continuous operation of the production line, leading him to believe that the tests accounted for the primary use of the production lines for most of the year and to question the validity of the claimed hours.
3. Client-Supplied Materials and Contractual Integration with Mabe/GE

In Projects 2007-01, 2007-02, and 2009-01, the parts being assembled (dryer motors, heating elements, and control panels) belonged to Mabe/GE, which supplied the materials directly to Les Abeilles. Furthermore, as noted at paragraph 28 of the judgment, Les Abeilles was required to obtain approval from Mabe/GE prior to performing experimental tests on the line, and subsequent pilot runs involved placing the assembled sub-components into dryers sold on the commercial market. Because the components were supplied by the client (Mabe/GE for three projects and, for Project 2009-02, the appellant's print-finishing client), Les Abeilles claimed almost no material expenditures (approximately $1,300 in Project 2007-01, $1,100 in Project 2007-02, $2,600 in Project 2009-01 and $300 in Project 2009-02 alongside ~$481,000 in salaries). Although the CRA's November 18, 2010 audit report made no reference to the almost complete absence of material expenses, Dr. Kooi repeatedly attached great importance to it during his testimony as an indicator that there was no experimental development—reasoning the Court could not understand, given that the material was supplied by the client.
4. Informal Documentation of Prior-Art Due Diligence

Before and during the experimental development work, the appellant sought existing solutions: for Projects 2007-01 and 2007-02, it drew on the Mabe/General Electric knowledge network (whose engineers could only provide general principles), its suppliers, Web searches and, for Project 2007-02, the manufacturer of the heating elements; for Project 2009-02, Mr. Caouette was unable to find an existing assembly line capable of performing the required work (a Chicago-based company reportedly had similar facilities but did not wish to share its knowledge); and for Project 2009-01, no existing software met the company's needs and the appellant's first-choice approach was too expensive to implement. Only after confirming that no existing commercial solution could satisfy their technical and cost parameters did Les Abeilles embark on developing custom internal processes. At the audit stage, however, the CRA's scientific advisor concluded (except for Project 2009-01) that the issues were engineering challenges whose solutions were based on current standard engineering practice by trial and error, and that some of the work related to the application of developed technology to a new situation.
The Crown's Fatal Legal, Methodological, and Evidentiary Failures at Trial
1. Elevating CRA Administrative Guidelines Above Statutory Law

A central flaw in the Crown's case was that its expert, Dr. Kooi, gave considerable importance to whether contemporaneous documentation existed as required by the CRA, effectively treating the CRA's internal administrative policies on contemporaneous documentation and the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion as mandatory statutory preconditions for SR&ED qualification. At paragraphs 94 through 98, Justice Jorré dismantled this position, ruling unequivocally that while the existence or content of contemporaneous documents is relevant to the Court's determination of a question of fact, the existence of contemporaneous documentation—or contemporaneous documents with specific content—is not a legal condition for the recognition of SR&ED. Quoting Judge Archambault in 116736 Canada inc. v. Canada ([1998] ACI No. 478 (QL)), Justice Jorré emphasized that although a taxpayer without contemporary test reports puts itself in a precarious position when trying to convince the Minister or the Court, neither the Income Tax Act nor the Regulations require written reports to be produced; it is possible to adduce evidence by way of oral testimony, in which case whether the activities were actually carried out becomes a question of credibility. Moreover, citing the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie, Justice Jorré confirmed that systematic research can be inferred where evidence establishes that work led to a technological advancement, and noted that part of the documentation was in fact contemporaneous, namely the "Chronology 2009" (a form of log), "Data" and "Perf Dos" tabs of the Excel spreadsheets in Exhibit A-12, derived from the appellant's database in which the data was collected as activities were being carried out.
2. Conflating Experimental Development with Pure or Applied Scientific Research

Throughout its assessment and trial argument, the Minister submitted that the appellant's activities involved no scientific uncertainty, were not based on a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology, and were merely routine activities involving no basic research, applied research or experimental development, and the respondent contended that the work amounted to the application of standard procedures or routine engineering (paragraphs 3 and 149). Justice Jorré rejected this position and focused the analysis on whether the projects constituted experimental development under paragraph (c) of the definition in subsection 248(1). Unlike basic research under paragraph (a) and applied research under paragraph (b), which explicitly require work undertaken for the "advancement of scientific knowledge," experimental development under paragraph (c) requires only work undertaken for the purpose of achieving "technological advancement" (progrès technologique) to create new or incrementally improve existing processes. At paragraphs 154 through 156 and 161, the Court found that there was technological uncertainty in Project 2007-01 because the appellant did not know at first how it would increase the production rate from every 14 seconds to every 9 seconds or produce all motors on the same line, Mabe/GE engineers could only provide general principles, and no ready-made solution could be found through its suppliers or Web searches, so that the appellant had to come up with its own solutions. In addition, the Court noted that the projects were aimed at increasing efficiency without excessive expense that the appellant could not support while remaining competitive (paragraph 11) and that the appellant came up with its own solutions at relatively modest cost (paragraph 156), and it recorded Mr. Gariépy's expert testimony that completing a project at a lower cost when the technology is available elsewhere at a greater cost can represent an advancement (paragraph 137); the Court did not, however, adopt cost-effectiveness as a stand-alone test of technological uncertainty or advancement.
3. Analytical Reductionism and Deconstruction of Multi-Year Projects

In evaluating Projects 2007-01, 2007-02, 2009-01, and 2009-02, the CRA's auditor took a narrow, piecemeal approach, examining each individual shop-floor test in isolation. Viewed individually, recalibrating an electronic relay to prevent contact fusing in Project 2007-01, adopting a cylinder system as the third of three successive solutions (after a manual solution requiring a special tool and a hybrid solution with a thumb detector) to solve the heating element proximity problem in Project 2007-02, or modifying the secondary feeder in Project 2009-02 could appear routine; indeed, the CRA's audit report characterized issues such as improvements to the pulley press hub, the alignment of motors and pulleys, and cycle time improvements in Project 2007-01 as engineering challenges solved by current standard engineering practice by trial and error. At paragraphs 150 through 153, Justice Jorré acknowledged that individual tests often do not appear, in and of themselves, to be a significant advancement, but held that it is important to consider each project globally in the year and not each test individually; while agreeing with the respondent that experimental development was required in the year in question, he held that this does not prevent examining the history of a project that began in a previous year (an approach urged by Mr. Gariépy, whose testimony is summarized at paragraphs 129 and 135). The Court held that systematically adjusting and modifying an automated manufacturing process across a coherent sequence of trials constitutes a systematic investigation (paragraphs 157–159), and that achieving increases in process productivity rates, operational stability, and line flexibility equates to technological advancement (paragraphs 147–148 and 162–163, consistent with Mr. Gariépy's testimony summarized at paragraphs 131–133), and that work may qualify even where its objectives are only partially attained or the work is unsuccessful, provided it was undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement (paragraph 143), as in Projects 2007-02, 2009-01 and 2009-02.
4. Lack of Independence, Role Confusion, and Gross Factual Errors by the Crown's Expert Witness

Five witnesses testified at the trial: Serge Caouette (president of the appellant), Yves Hamelin (president of Groupe HLP, who testified regarding the audit and objection process), Dr. Martin Gariépy (expert witness for the appellant, holding a Bachelor of Science in Pure Mathematics, a Master's in Aerospace Engineering, and a Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering), Dr. Steven Kooi (the CRA science advisor who audited the claim and was tendered as the Crown's expert witness, holding a Bachelor's in Chemical Engineering and a Master's and Doctorate in Mechanical Engineering), and Denis Frayce (Dr. Kooi's supervisor at the CRA).

Justice Jorré's critique of Dr. Kooi's expert report (Exhibit I-3) and oral testimony was devastating to the Crown's defence. First, Justice Jorré explicitly concluded that "Mr. Kooi was not impartial". During both his testimony and in his written report, Dr. Kooi exhibited a fundamental confusion between his role as a CRA scientific adviser during the audit and his role as an expert witness before the Court. While it is normal for a scientific adviser at the audit stage to be guided by internal CRA policies and administrative proof standards, an expert witness must offer an independent opinion grounded in personal technical expertise; Dr. Kooi instead appeared guided primarily by CRA administrative guidelines. Second, Dr. Kooi improperly usurped the judicial fact-finding role by writing in his expert report that "The information provided concerning project 2009-02 was false," prompting Justice Jorré to point out that determining the veracity of evidence is a question of fact exclusively for the Court, not a matter of expert opinion. Third, Dr. Kooi committed severe arithmetic and operational errors when interpreting the taxpayer's database logs. He confused aggregate person-hours of labour with continuous machine test duration, mistakenly assuming that production tests 2456 and 2282 ran continuously 24 hours a day, 7 days a week for the equivalent of 11 and 26 days, respectively, whereas the 627.25 figure for test 2282 represented person-hours of work rather than hours of testing, and the test actually lasted only a fraction of that time. Similarly, his report stated that 56 persons were involved in test 2282, a figure he himself corrected to 28 at the beginning of his testimony, and the evidence showed that those 28 persons were involved at different times over the course of the test rather than all being present at the same time. Finally, Dr. Kooi repeatedly relied on the absence of material expenses claimed by Les Abeilles as proof that no experimental development occurred, overlooking the fact that the material was supplied by the client (Mabe/GE for three of the four projects). By contrast, the Court accepted parts of Dr. Gariépy's testimony, notably that there was a systematic investigation (paragraph 157), while noting that his report was relatively general (paragraph 86), that whether the projects constitute SR&ED is a question for the Court rather than for expert opinion (paragraph 84), and that it would have been useful to have expert evidence focused more specifically on the current state of practices and knowledge respecting assembly methods and techniques (paragraph 85).
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen against the taxpayer's pre-litigation vulnerabilities, the CRA's audit-stage challenge and trial failures, and the governing legal standard of proof articulated by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Audit-Stage Vulnerability and CRA's Challenge
Court's Standard of Proof and Final Holding in Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313)

cells: 1. Technological Risk or Uncertainty (Criterion 1 of Northwest Hydraulic)
ITA s. 248(1) definition of SR&ED, para. (c); Northwest Hydraulic (98 DTC 1839); CW Agencies (2001 FCA 393)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Conducted prior-art due diligence via informal internet searches and oral consultations with internal/client networks without archiving formal feasibility reports. CRA Challenge: Concluded at audit (except for Project 2009-01) that the issues were engineering challenges whose solutions were based on current standard engineering practice by trial and error, involving the application of developed technology to a new situation.

Standard of Proof: Technological uncertainty was found where the appellant did not know at the outset how it would achieve its specific production objectives and the work could not be characterized as standard procedures or routine engineering (paras. 154–156, 161). Holding: The appellant's unsuccessful attempts to find ready-made solutions through the Mabe/GE knowledge network, its suppliers and Web searches formed part of the evidence supporting the finding of uncertainty (paras. 155, 177). The Court noted the projects' aim of efficiency without excessive expense (para. 11) and the relatively modest cost of the solutions (para. 156); the view that a lower-cost solution can represent an advancement came from Mr. Gariépy's testimony (para. 137).
2. Formulation of Hypotheses and Systematic Investigation (Criteria 2 and 3 of Northwest Hydraulic)
ITA s. 248(1) preamble ("systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis"); RIS-Christie (99 DTC 5087)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Executed iterative modifications directly on shop-floor assembly lines (22 tests in 2009-01; 13 tests in 2009-02) without academic lab protocols. CRA Challenge: Looked at the projects test by test, deconstructing them into isolated shop-floor tests, claiming each individual relay, stop, or feeder adjustment was routine troubleshooting.

Standard of Proof: Each project must be considered globally in the year at issue and not test by test; the history of a project that began in a previous year may be examined, but experimental development must be carried out in the year in question (paras. 150–153). Holding: Iterative design, testing, and modification of a manufacturing process (e.g., three successive solutions to the heating element proximity problem in 2007-02, culminating in a cylinder system; the "surgeon approach" in 2009-01) constituted a systematic investigation in which hypotheses were formulated and the scientific method applied, in all four projects (paras. 157–158).
3. Technological Advancement in Experimental Development (Criterion 4 of Northwest Hydraulic)
ITA s. 248(1) para. (c) ("achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing... processes, including incremental improvements")

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Articulated project goals around production rate increases (9-sec motor cycle in 2007-01; 11,000/hr print speed in 2009-02) and line flexibility (174 panel variants in 2009-01). CRA Challenge: Submitted that the activities involved no scientific uncertainty and were merely routine activities, amounting to the application of standard procedures or routine engineering (paras. 3, 149).

Standard of Proof: Unlike basic or applied research under paras. (a)–(b) which require scientific knowledge advancement, experimental development under para. (c) requires only technological progress, including incremental process improvements (paras. 8, 138–140). Holding: Increases in productivity rate, stability, and flexibility of a manufacturing process constitute technological advancement (paras. 147–148, 162–163); work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement may qualify even if unsuccessful or only partially successful (paras. 143, 168, 173, 177).
4. Exclusion of Commercial Production and Routine Testing (Statutory Exclusions)
ITA s. 248(1) paras. (f) (quality control or routine testing) and (i) (commercial production or commercial use of a process)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Shop-floor tests required at least as many employees as regular commercial production (e.g., 28 persons involved at different times in test 2282) and used client-supplied parts (Mabe/GE for three projects; the appellant's client for 2009-02), resulting in minimal material claims ($300 to $2,600 per project). CRA Challenge: Crown expert read person-hours as hours of continuous 24/7 line operation (e.g., 627.25 person-hours on test 2282 read as 26 days of testing, and test 2456 as 11 days) and, in testimony, repeatedly treated near-zero material claims as an indicator against experimental development.

Standard of Proof: Only category (c) experimental development deviations were at issue; the first-piece and pilot-run stages, during which parts were placed in dryers sold on the market, took place after testing and were not part of what was at issue (paras. 26–27, 34–35). Holding: Stages after experimental testing (pilot runs) were properly excluded from the claim (para. 35). The Court could not understand why the absence of material expenses, where material was supplied by the client, would indicate no experimental development (note 57); the claimed hours were person-hours, consistent with Mr. Caouette's testimony that a test required at least as many employees as regular production (paras. 36, 109).
5. Contemporaneous Documentation and Record-Keeping (Criterion 5 of Northwest Hydraulic)
ITA s. 248(1); 116736 Canada inc. ([1998] ACI No. 478 (QL)); RIS-Christie (99 DTC 5087)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Lacked dedicated SR&ED technical reports drafted during the work; relied on ERP database tabs ("Chronology 2009", "Data" barcode scans, "Perf Dos") and post-hoc trial summaries. CRA Challenge: Crown expert gave considerable importance to whether contemporaneous documentation existed as required by the CRA and asserted that no contemporaneous log was kept, although his November 18, 2010 audit report made no mention of a lack of contemporaneous documents (paras. 92, 120).

Standard of Proof: Contemporaneous documentation—or contemporaneous documents with specific content—is not a statutory condition for SR&ED recognition (para. 94); it is an evidentiary matter of weight and credibility. Holding: Part of the documentation was contemporaneous (Exhibit A-12 tabs "Chronology 2009", "Data" and "Perf Dos"; Exhibits A-3 and A-4), and the non-contemporaneous project and test descriptions, filed by consent and unchallenged, remained detailed evidence of the projects; together with the testimony, this evidence established experimental development (paras. 94, 121–122, notes 41, 59 and 77).
6. Independence and Reliability of Expert Testimony (Evidentiary and Procedural Standard)
Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), SOR/90-688a; Hospira Healthcare Corporation v. Eli Lilly Canada Inc., 2010 FCA 282 (cited at note 36 on impartiality versus independence)

CRA Failure at Trial: Tendered its own auditing science advisor (Dr. Steven Kooi) as an expert witness; Dr. Kooi relied on CRA policy guidelines rather than personal expertise, declared taxpayer facts "false," and made gross arithmetic errors.

Standard of Proof: What matters is the expert's impartiality rather than independence; being a CRA employee is not in itself sufficient to refuse recognition as an expert, but an expert must form his or her own opinion based on personal expertise rather than be guided by CRA guidelines (paras. 83, 90, note 36). Holding: Crown expert held not impartial and given very little weight (paras. 97, 114), without the Court needing to rule on the objection to his recognition (para. 83); the Appellant's expert (Dr. Martin Gariépy) produced a relatively general report, though the Court accepted his testimony on systematic investigation (paras. 86, 157); costs were awarded to the Appellant.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

While Les Abeilles confirmed that a Canadian taxpayer can prevail before the Tax Court of Canada through credible oral testimony, operational ERP time-scans, and independent expert testimony, relying on litigation to rescue an SR&ED claim is financially costly and operationally perilous. As Judge Archambault cautioned in 116736 Canada inc. v. Canada (quoted with approval by Justice Jorré), a taxpayer contesting the Minister's refusal to allow R&D expenditures without contemporary written reports showing detailed records of each experiment places itself in a "very precarious position" in which, absent such reports, whether the activities were actually carried out becomes a question of credibility.

The following two applied remedial case studies demonstrate how Canadian industrial taxpayers confronting the exact operational, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls identified in Les Abeilles can proactively restructure their project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and shop-floor experimentation tracking to satisfy CRA audit scrutiny and the statutory mandate of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act.
Case Study 1: Automotive Tier-2 EV Battery Module Sub-Assembly (Overcoming Shop-Floor Production Overlap and Client-Supplied Material Pitfalls)
Operational Scenario and Pitfall Alignment

Laurentian Powertrain Assemblies Inc. ("Laurentian"), a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation based in Trois-Rivières, Québec, sub-assembles structural thermal-management plates and cell-interconnect modules for an Original Equipment Manufacturer ("OEM") assembling electric commercial vehicles in Canada. To prevent the OEM from offshoring the sub-assembly contract to a lower-wage facility in Mexico, Laurentian undertakes an ambitious process development project in 2026 to engineer a single, flexible pull-flow assembly line using electronic sequencing capable of assembling 48 distinct battery module variations from 450 sub-components within a three-hour order turnaround window, while compressing station cycle speed from 22 seconds down to 10 seconds per module. Under the supply arrangement, the OEM supplies all lithium-ion pouch cells and aluminum cooling manifolds on a consigned basis at zero material cost to Laurentian, and Laurentian must obtain prior engineering sign-off from the OEM before running any non-standard assembly trial. During the year, Laurentian conducts 20 shop-floor trials accumulating 7,500 person-hours across a 24-person assembly crew to resolve severe false-reject spikes at the automated optical and ultrasonic weld-inspection station caused by high-speed mechanical indexing impacts against the station stop. Laurentian claims $320,000 in salaries and only $1,100 in sacrificial fixture materials.

This scenario replicates the exact audit vulnerabilities of Projects 2007-01, 2007-02, and 2009-01 in Les Abeilles. Without structural remediation, a CRA Research and Technology Advisor is highly likely to disallow the claim on four grounds: asserting that cycle-speed compression and kitting flexibility are commercial productivity goals rather than technological advancements; pointing to the OEM's prior approval requirement and the near-zero material expenditure claim ($1,100) as evidence of routine contract manufacturing; confusing the 7,500 person-hours across 24 workers with continuous commercial production excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i) or routine quality control excluded under paragraph 248(1)(f); and deconstructing the 20 trials into isolated mechanical stop and relay adjustments deemed to be routine engineering.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Project Governance Restructuring via a Formal Three-Tier Deviation Gate Protocol

Laurentian must institutionalize and upgrade the three-tier deviation governance model examined by Justice Jorré at paragraphs 26 through 35 of Les Abeilles by embedding a formal SR&ED Deviation Gate Protocol directly within its plant Quality Management System. Under this protocol, every non-standard shop-floor intervention must be classified prior to execution into one of three mutually exclusive ERP project codes: DEV-A for routine component substitutions, DEV-B for standard engineering adjustments (such as routine PLC calibration or fixture shimming within established equipment specifications), and DEV-C-SRED exclusively for experimental development trials aimed at resolving a documented system-level technological uncertainty. Only DEV-C-SRED activities are eligible to accumulate hours toward the SR&ED tax credit pool. Crucially, to respect the exclusion in paragraph 248(1)(i) and mirror the separation noted at paragraph 35 of Les Abeilles, the governance charter must institute an automated "Gate Cut-Off" the moment the third-generation automated damping stop eliminates the false rejects at the 10-second cycle target. All subsequent OEM validation runs, Production Part Approval Process (PPAP) runs, and pilot production runs where modules are placed into commercial vehicles for sale on the market are automatically diverted to a commercial cost centre (PROD-PILOT) and strictly excluded from the SR&ED claim.
Step 2: Technical Documentation Restructuring via Due Diligence Archives and Holistic Phase Matrices

To neutralize the CRA's "routine engineering" and "test deconstruction" objections during the audit stage without waiting for trial testimony, Laurentian must restructure its technical documentation at two levels. First, prior to authorizing the initial DEV-C-SRED trial, the lead manufacturing engineer must compile a contemporaneous Baseline Technological Uncertainty and Due Diligence Dossier that formalizes the kind of internet searches and consultations described by Justice Jorré at paragraphs 155 and 177 of Les Abeilles. This dossier archives equipment vendor specifications proving that standard indexing stops fail below 16-second cycle times, records written minutes of consultations with OEM and external automation engineers confirming that no known off-the-shelf damping solution fits within Laurentian's spatial and commercial cost constraints (cf. paragraphs 11 and 156, and Mr. Gariépy's testimony at paragraph 137), and defines why the dynamic coupling between high-speed pull-flow indexing and ultrasonic test-station impact cannot be resolved through standard procedures. Second, to prevent the CRA from dissecting the 20 shop-floor trials into isolated routine adjustments, Laurentian must maintain a unified Master Experimental Matrix that groups individual trials into sequential, hypothesis-driven experimental generations (mirroring the progression of three successive solutions—manual with a special tool, hybrid with a thumb detector, and a cylinder system—to the heating element proximity problem in Project 2007-02 and the "surgeon approach" trials in Project 2009-01, per paragraphs 55, 60–62 and 150–153). Each entry in the matrix explicitly connects the physical modification made on the shop floor to the overarching multi-year technological objective, ensuring the project is evaluated holistically.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring of Customer Approval Rights and Consigned Material Clauses

To prevent a CRA auditor from repeating Dr. Kooi's error of treating near-zero material claims as an indicator against experimental development, and to forestall any similar argument based on customer sign-offs, Laurentian must execute a Manufacturing Process R&D Addendum to its supply agreement with the OEM. The addendum must explicitly stipulate three legal and operational facts: first, that while the OEM owns the product design of the battery module and supplies the raw cells and manifolds on a consigned bailment basis for testing, Laurentian acts as an independent contractor bearing 100% of the financial and technical risk of conceiving, developing, and optimizing the automated sub-assembly process; second, that all intellectual property, process patents, and trade secrets generated in the sub-assembly process, pull-flow electronic sequencing software, and custom test-station stops vest solely in Laurentian; and third, that the OEM's prior approval of DEV-C-SRED test requests (as described at paragraph 28 of Les Abeilles) constitutes strictly a product-quality and safety authorization permitting consigned OEM parts to pass through modified tooling, rather than technical direction or funding of Laurentian's SR&ED. In its Form T661 claim package, Laurentian's tax advisor should include an explicit financial disclosure note citing Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313) to explain why material claims are limited to the $1,100 of custom-machined stop prototypes consumed in testing while core components were supplied free of charge by the client.
Step 4: Experimentation and ERP Time-Tracking Restructuring to Prevent Auditor Arithmetic Errors

To eliminate any possibility of a CRA reviewer confusing aggregate person-hours with continuous 24/7 machine runtime—the exact mathematical blunder committed by Dr. Kooi regarding tests 2456 and 2282 in Les Abeilles—Laurentian must upgrade its ERP barcode time-tracking architecture (analogous to the "Data" and "Perf Dos" tabs in Exhibit A-12). Whenever a DEV-C-SRED trial is executed, the ERP database must generate a dual-ledger record that separates Chronological Line Window Duration (for example, logging that the assembly line was halted for commercial production and dedicated to Test 2026-14 on November 12 from 08:00 to 14:00, representing 6.0 elapsed machine hours) from Aggregate Employee Person-Hours (logging the individual barcode badge scans of the 24 operators, kitting specialists, and automation engineers who staffed the stations across staggered intervals during that window, totaling 144.0 person-hours). Each test ledger entry must also include a mandatory supervisor sign-off certifying that full-line staffing was physically necessary to replicate real-time pull-flow kitting queues and harmonic line inertia during the experimental trial, directly reflecting Mr. Caouette's testimony, recounted at paragraph 36 of Les Abeilles, that a test required at least as many employees as regular commercial production.
Case Study 2: High-Speed Sustainable Packaging and Print Finishing Line (Overcoming Situation-Specific Uncertainty, Partial Success, and Retroactive Documentation Pitfalls)
Operational Scenario and Pitfall Alignment

Boréal Éco-Conditionnement Inc. ("Boréal"), an industrial packaging and print finishing corporation located in Drummondville, Québec, undertakes an internal experimental development project in 2026 to synchronize the high-speed application of biodegradable secondary barrier components onto printed paperboard cartons. To keep its packaging contracts competitive in Canada, Boréal seeks to increase secondary component application speed by over 80%—from 6,000 applications per hour to 11,000 applications per hour—while simultaneously re-engineering its rotary secondary feeder to accommodate larger component geometries and introduce new secondary packaging elements. Before starting the project, Boréal's plant engineers search technical databases on the internet and consult press manufacturers, confirming that no existing commercial retrofit kit can handle the aerodynamic flutter and adhesive shear of larger biodegradable secondary components above 6,500 units per hour on Boréal's existing mechanical cam-driven press architecture. Across the fiscal year, Boréal conducts 13 shop-floor experimental trials investing 6,200 person-hours of labour ($78,000 in salaries and $400 in modified feeder guide materials). By year-end, Boréal successfully modifies the secondary feeder to feed the larger component formats and new secondary components reliably, but maximum synchronized application speed reaches only 8,900 applications per hour—falling short of the 11,000/hour objective. Furthermore, Boréal's shop-floor supervisors record only raw chronological database timestamps and barcode badge scans during the year, relying on an external SR&ED consultant to draft detailed project and test descriptions eight months after fiscal year-end.

This scenario mirrors the exact factual and legal posture of Project 2009-02 in Les Abeilles. On audit, the CRA is predisposed to deny the claim in full on three grounds: alleging that modifying an existing print-finishing feeder to run faster and accept larger components is routine machine adaptation lacking genuine scientific or technological uncertainty; arguing that failing to reach the 11,000 applications per hour target demonstrates an absence of technological advancement; and rejecting the consultant's retroactive technical narratives while dismissing the raw ERP database timestamps as insufficient contemporaneous documentation under the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Governance Restructuring Around Situation-Specific Uncertainty and Partial Year-End Advancement

Boréal must align its internal R&D project charter directly with Justice Jorré's statutory interpretation of paragraph 248(1)(c) at paragraphs 140, 143, 154–156, and 162–163 of Les Abeilles. Rather than allowing its claim to be judged against the standard of basic or applied scientific research under paragraphs 248(1)(a) and (b), Boréal's project governance charter must explicitly frame the project around situation-specific technological uncertainty constrained by commercial cost-effectiveness. At project inception, the engineering committee must record a formal Project Initiation Protocol documenting two foundational facts: first, that while purchasing a brand-new $3.5 million linear-motor packaging line could theoretically achieve 11,000 applications per hour, such a capital expenditure is commercially unviable for Boréal's production volume, creating a situation-specific technological uncertainty as to whether aerodynamic boundary-layer separation and cam harmonic vibration on the existing mechanical rotary feeder can be overcome within a $90,000 retrofit envelope (invoking paragraphs 11 and 154–156, and Mr. Gariépy's testimony at paragraph 137); and second, that achieving incremental process improvements—including intermediate speed gains from 6,000 to 8,900 applications per hour and successful adaptation of the secondary feeder for larger component formats—constitutes qualifying technological advancement under paragraph 248(1)(c) even if the ultimate 11,000/hour speed target requires continued experimentation in the subsequent fiscal year.
Step 2: Technical Documentation Restructuring via Embedded ERP Micro-Logs

While Justice Jorré held at paragraph 94 of Les Abeilles that contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific content, is not a condition to the recognition of SR&ED, relying on post-hoc summaries admitted by consent at trial exposes a taxpayer to unnecessary audit denials and litigation costs. To bridge the gap between raw operational database tables ("Chronology 2009", "Data", and "Perf Dos" in Exhibit A-12) and formal technical narratives without imposing onerous paperwork on press operators, Boréal must embed a four-field Experimental Test Micro-Log directly into its shop-floor ERP interface for each of the 13 trials:

items: Prior-Art & Hypothesis Field: A mandatory two-sentence entry completed by the lead technician before the press starts, stating the specific hypothesis being tested in that trial (for example, Test 09: Modifying vacuum manifold dwell angle by +6 degrees and installing Venturi relief slots to prevent larger secondary components from skewing above 8,500 units/hr).

Physical Configuration & Material Link: Automated capture of the $400 in custom-milled feeder guide prototypes installed for the trial, coupled with time-stamped digital photographs of the feeder setup.

Automated Press Telemetry Export: Direct digital logging from the press controller capturing exact test start and stop timestamps, peak application rate achieved (8,900/hr), registration variance in millimetres, and jam frequency.

Contemporaneous Analytical Conclusion: A mandatory three-sentence post-run entry explaining why the test succeeded in feeding larger components but failed to sustain 11,000 applications per hour (such as adhesive tailing caused by insufficient thermal curing dwell time at higher web velocity), automatically linking Test 09 to the hypothesis formulated for Test 10.

body.text: Step 3: Contractual Restructuring of External Technical Consultant Engagements

Because small and medium-sized Canadian manufacturers frequently engage specialized SR&ED consulting firms (such as Groupe HLP, whose president Yves Hamelin testified in Les Abeilles) to assist with claim preparation, Boréal must restructure its consulting engagement contract to eliminate the "retroactive documentation" vulnerability. Instead of retaining the consultant after fiscal year-end to write retrospective technical narratives from memory, Boréal's contract with its SR&ED advisor must mandate quarterly contemporaneous technical audits at the end of each fiscal quarter. Under these contract terms, the external advisor reviews the raw ERP "Chronology", "Data" barcode scans, and Experimental Test Micro-Logs every 90 days while the work is in progress, verifying that all 13 tests are cross-linked to payroll records and signed off by Boréal's internal press supervisor within 15 days of each trial. Consequently, when the Form T661 technical narrative is compiled at year-end, it functions strictly as an index and synthesis of pre-existing, date-stamped contemporaneous engineering records rather than a retroactive reconstruction.
Step 4: Audit Defence and Litigation Readiness Protocol

Finally, Boréal must establish an internal SR&ED Audit and Dispute Resolution Protocol calibrated to the evidentiary holdings of Les Abeilles. If the CRA selects Boréal's claim for a technical review, Boréal must ensure that the press supervisor and plant president who personally directed the 13 trials lead the technical walkthrough, presenting the contemporaneous ERP database links ("Chronology", "Data" badge scans, and "Perf Dos" metrics) alongside physical samples of the modified secondary feeder components. If the CRA RTA issues a draft science report proposing to disallow the claim on the basis of internal CRA policy definitions of "state of technology" or alleged deficiencies in documentation format, Boréal's tax counsel must file a formal administrative rebuttal citing paragraphs 94, 140, and 150–164 of Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313). Furthermore, should the dispute proceed to the Tax Court of Canada, Boréal must retain a credentialed, fully independent external engineering expert (mirroring Dr. Martin Gariépy's role in Les Abeilles) to map the 13 shop-floor trials onto the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, while formally challenging the impartiality and weight of any in-house CRA auditor tendered by the Crown as an expert witness.

Holistic project evaluation (paras. 150–153); efficiency without excessive expense and modest cost (paras. 11, 156; expert testimony at para. 137); documentation weight vs. statutory conditions (para. 94).
Governance Architecture

Technical Documentation

Contractual Structure

body.text: 5. Strategic Synthesis for Canadian SR&ED Counsel and Technical Advisors

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313) represents a vital judicial check on administrative overreach in the administration of Canada's SR&ED tax incentive program. By grounding its analysis in the statutory language of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and in the evidentiary guidance of the Federal Court of Appeal (that systematic research may be inferred where it is established that such research led to a technological advancement) in RIS-Christie, Justice Jorré confirmed that experimental development in Canada is not restricted to white-coat laboratory research or breakthroughs in global scientific theory. Rather, paragraph 248(1)(c) encompasses systematic, iterative shop-floor experimentation undertaken by Canadian manufacturers to overcome technological uncertainties in their industrial processes, even where the underlying objective is increased production efficiency. When corporate taxpayers combine the legal protections of Les Abeilles with disciplined deviation gating, contemporaneous ERP cross-linking, clear contractual risk allocation, and independent technical expertise, shop-floor process development claims can be defended with exceptional authority at both the CRA audit stage and before the Tax Court of Canada.

outcome: Appeal allowed with costs; shop-floor process work qualified and contemporaneous documentation is not a statutory condition.
